The reedfish, Erpetoichthys calabaricus, is a remarkable actinopterygian native to West African swamps, and its reproductive strategy reflects the hydrological constraints of its habitat. A single female can produce between 800 and 1200 eggs per clutch [N_R_i = between 800 and 1200 eggs per clutch] over the course of a year, completing approximately 3 to 4 clutches annually [F_R_i = approximately 3 to 4 clutches annually] when maintained at a water temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This relatively high fecundity is typical of polypteriform species, which produce large clutches to offset the intense predation pressure on the early life stages. The developing embryos are deposited in vegetative refugia, where they adhere firmly to submerged surfaces. Following a brief incubation period, the yolk-sac larva emerges and relies entirely on its endogenous yolk reserves for the first several days of life before initiating exogenous feeding.

Newly hatched reedfish prolarvae measure approximately one centimeter [Lb = approximately one centimeter] in total length, a modest size at emergence that underscores the altricial nature of the earliest larval phase. The hatchling emerges at just 3 days after egg deposition , a surprisingly rapid eclosion that allows the prolarva to evacuate the egg chorion and begin a sedentary, yolk-dependent existence at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. The incubation temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C] is crucial for this early ontogeny, as it accelerates the hatching process and the subsequent yolk absorption. Once the yolk sac is fully resorbed, the larva transitions to an exotrophic feeding mode at an age at birth of 19 days [ab = 19 days], marking the onset of active foraging behavior at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C].

Growth during the juvenile phase is notably rapid under the controlled thermal conditions optimal for this species. At five months of age, young reedfish have been recorded reaching a total length of 6 centimeters , which signifies an impressive developmental achievement for a fish born at just one centimeter at a temperature of 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. This trajectory is sustained when water temperatures are maintained at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], allowing for efficient metabolic processing of the invertebrate prey that constitutes the bulk of their diet. The sustained growth rate underpins the eventual achievement of the large body sizes observed in mature specimens, which is supported by the abundant food resources in nutrient-rich environments that characterize their swampy habitats.

Female reedfish undergo gonadal development during a prolonged sub-adult phase, ultimately achieving sexual maturation at approximately 6 years after hatching [tR = approximately 6 years after hatching], when water temperatures remain at a consistent 26 °C [T = 26 °C]. At this point, a typical female attains a total length of 31.4 centimeters [Lp = 31.4 centimeters] and a corresponding wet weight of 36.7 grams [Wwp = 36.7 grams], a body mass that represents the threshold for initiating reproductive activity. The timing of first reproduction is a critical life-history event, as it balances the need for continued somatic expansion against the energetic demands of spawning. Studies comparing captive and wild populations suggest that this schedule is relatively fixed, although minor variations are observed depending on local food availability.

The maximum documented lifespan for the reedfish extends to 20 years [am = 20 years] under the stable captive conditions typical of these experiments at 26 °C [T = 26 °C], a longevity that places it among the more slowly aging members of the Polypteridae. This protracted lifespan, coupled with delayed maturity and slow growth, reflects a life-history strategy that favors survival and iteroparity over rapid turnover, a pattern common among large-bodied aquatic predators in stable, resource-poor environments. Fully grown females can attain an ultimate total length of 37 centimeters [Li = 37 centimeters], and their corresponding ultimate wet weight reaches 60.4 grams [Wwi = 60.4 grams], a substantial mass for a fish of its body plan. The protracted lifespan of the reedfish, coupled with its delayed maturity and impressive maximal size, illustrates a life-history strategy that relies on steady, continuous growth and a relatively low annual reproductive output despite the high fecundity per event.
